arXiv:1708.07258v2 [math-ph] 25 Aug 2017

Numerical calculation of N-periodic wave solutions to coupled KdV-type equations

Yingnan Zhang    Xingbiao Hu    Jianqing Sun ††thanks: sunjq@lsec.cc.ac.cn
Abstract

In this paper, we study periodic wave solutions of coupled KdV-type equations. We present a numerical process to calculate the NN-periodic waves based on the direct method of calculating periodic wave solutions proposed by Akira Nakamura. Particularly, in the case of N=1,2,3N=1,2,3, we give some detailed examples to show the N-periodic wave solutions to a coupled Ramani equation.

 1Jiangsu Key Laboratory for NSLSCS, School of Mathematical Sciences, Nanjing Normal University, Nanjing, China

 2LSEC, Institute of Computational Mathematics and Scientific Engineering Computing, Academy of Mathematics and Systems Sciences, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China

Keywords: N-periodic wave solution, coupled KdV-type equation, Riemann’s theta-function, Gauss-Newton method

1 Introduction

In this paper, we focus on numerical calculation of NN-periodic wave solutions to coupled KdV-type soliton equations. The periodic solution mentioned here represents periodic analogue of soliton solution, and in general case NN-periodic wave solution is a periodic generalization of NN-soliton solution or multiple collision of NN solitons[18].

Much work has already been done on periodic waves. The pioneering work was made by Novikov and Dubrovin[2, 3, 4], Lax[5], Its and Matveev[6], McKean and Moerbeke[7] in 1970s. After that, some classical methods such as the inverse scattering method[8, 9, 10], the algebro-geometric approach[11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17] and the direct method[18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23], are applied to solve periodic waves. However, comparing with soliton waves, the periodic waves are more complicated and it is difficult to give some detailed explicit expressions. Therefore, many researchers turn to numerical calculations. Recent work includes the numerical approach via Riemann-Hilbert problem[24, 25] and spectral method[26, 27, 28]. Here we will calculate the periodic waves numerically based on the direct method[1, 18, 19, 20].

In Refs. [18]-[19], Nakamura first proposed the conditions for having NN-periodic waves to nonlinear evolution equation which can be reduced to some certain type of bilinear equations, such as KdV, mKdV, NLS and some other equations. And then in Ref. [20], Hirota suggested researchers investigate whether the soliton equations written in bilinear form exhibit 33-periodic wave solutions or not by this condition.

In this paper, we will apply the conditions to coupled KdV-type equations and give a numerical procedure to calculate their NN-periodic wave solutions. Here “coupled KdV-type” means that, with some suitable variable transformations and auxiliary variables, equation can be transformed into the following bilinear form

F1​(Dt,Dz,Dx,⋯,c1)​f⋅f=0,\displaystyle F_{1}(D_{t},D_{z},D_{x},\cdots,c_{1})f\cdot f=0, (1.1)
F2​(Dt,Dz,Dx,⋯,c2)​f⋅f=0,\displaystyle F_{2}(D_{t},D_{z},D_{x},\cdots,c_{2})f\cdot f=0, (1.2)

where F1,F2F_{1},F_{2} are even functions of Dt,Dz,Dx,⋯,D_{t},D_{z},D_{x},\cdots, c1,c2c_{1},c_{2} are integral constants, and the DD operator[1] is defined by

Dtm​Dxn​a​(t,x)⋅b⁡(t,x)\displaystyle D_{t}^{m}D_{x}^{n}a(t,x)\cdot b(t,x) (1.3)
=\displaystyle= ∂m∂sm​∂n∂yn​a​(t+s,x+y)​b​(t−s,x−y)|s=0,y=0,\displaystyle\frac{\partial^{m}}{\partial s^{m}}\frac{\partial^{n}}{\partial y^{n}}a(t+s,x+y)b(t-s,x-y)|_{s=0,y=0},
m,n=0,1,2,⋯.\displaystyle m,n=0,1,2,\cdots.

Many soliton equations can be viewed as coupled KdV-type equations. For example, the coupled Ramani equation[31]

ux​x​x​x​x​x+15​ux​x​ux​x​x+15​ux​ux​x​x​x+45​ux2​ux​x\displaystyle u_{xxxxxx}+15u_{xx}u_{xxx}+15u_{x}u_{xxxx}+45u_{x}^{2}u_{xx}
−5​(ux​x​x​t+3​ux​x​ut+3​ux​ux​t)−5​ut​t+18​vx=0,\displaystyle\quad-5(u_{xxxt}+3u_{xx}u_{t}+3u_{x}u_{xt})-5u_{tt}+18v_{x}=0, (1.4)
vt−vx​x​x−3​vx​ux−3​v​ux​x=0,\displaystyle v_{t}-v_{xxx}-3v_{x}u_{x}-3vu_{xx}=0, (1.5)

can be transformed into the bilinear form

(Dx6−5​Dx3​Dt−5​Dt2+9​Dx​Dz+c1)​f⋅f=0,\displaystyle(D_{x}^{6}-5D_{x}^{3}D_{t}-5D_{t}^{2}+9D_{x}D_{z}+c_{1})f\cdot f=0, (1.6)
(Dz​Dt−Dz​Dx3−6​v0​Dx2+c2)​f⋅f=0,\displaystyle(D_{z}D_{t}-D_{z}D_{x}^{3}-6v_{0}D_{x}^{2}+c_{2})f\cdot f=0, (1.7)

by the dependent variable transformation

u=u0+(ln​f)x​x,v=v0+(ln​f)x​z,u=u_{0}+(\mathrm{ln}f)_{xx},\quad v=v_{0}+(\mathrm{ln}f)_{xz}, (1.8)

where zz is an auxiliary variable and c1,c2c_{1},c_{2} are integral constants. This type of equations also include the Hirota-Satsuma coupled KdV equation[32], the Camassa-Holm equation[33, 34], the semi-discrete KdV equation[35] and some other discrete soliton equations[36, 37].

In the case of single KdV-type bilinear equations, as shown by Nakamura[18] and Hirota[20], there are always exactly 11- and 22- periodic wave solutions and if N≥3N\geq 3, we need solve an over-determined nonlinear algebraic system to obtain a NN-periodic wave. However, the situation of coupled KdV-type equations is different. In this case, there are only exactly 11-periodic wave solutions and if N≥2N\geq 2, it is necessary for us to deal with an over-determined algebraic system to solve NN-periodic wave solutions( see Sect. 2 for details).

The paper is organized as follows. In Sect. 2, we will review the conditions given by Nakamura and apply them to the coupled KdV-type bilinear Eqs. (1.1)-(1.2). In Sect. 3, we will propose a numerical procedure by using Gauss-Newton method based on the condition. Section 4 devotes to some numerical results of the coupled Ramani Eqs.  (1.6)-(1.7). Some conclusions and discussions will be given in Sect. 5.

2 Condition for NN-periodic wave solutions

Firstly, we review the Riemann’s θ\theta-function defined by

θ(𝜼;𝒔|𝝉)=∑m1∑m2⋯∑mN=−∞∞exp[i∑j=1N(mj+sj)ηj\displaystyle\theta({\bm{\eta}};{\bm{s}}|{\bm{\tau}})=\sum_{m_{1}}\sum_{m_{2}}\cdots\sum_{m_{N}=-\infty}^{\infty}\exp[i\sum_{j=1}^{N}(m_{j}+s_{j})\eta_{j}
−12∑j,k=1N(mj+sj)τj,k(mk+sk)],\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j,k=1}^{N}(m_{j}+s_{j})\tau_{j,k}(m_{k}+s_{k})], (2.9)

where ηj\eta_{j}, sjs_{j} and τj,k\tau_{j,k} are the elements of the vector 𝜼\bm{\eta}, 𝒔\bm{s} and the symmetric matrix 𝝉\bm{\tau} respectively, and ηj\eta_{j} is defined by

ηj=ωjt+kjx+⋯+ηj0,j=1,2,⋯N.\eta_{j}=\omega_{j}t+k_{j}x+\cdots+\eta_{j}^{0},\quad j=1,2,\cdots N. (2.10)

Here kjk_{j}, ωj\omega_{j}, ηj0\eta_{j}^{0}, the diagonal elements τj​j\tau_{jj} and off-diagonal elements τj​k,j≠k\tau_{jk},j\neq k are parameters corresponding to the wave numbers, the frequencies, the phase positions, the amplitudes and the interactions respectively.

2.1 Single KdV-type bilinear equations

For a single KdV-type bilinear equation

F⁡(Dt,Dx,⋯,λ)​f⋅f=0,F(D_{t},D_{x},\cdots,\lambda)f\cdot f=0, (2.11)

the condition for having NN-periodic wave solutions was first proposed by Nakamura[18].

Lemma 2.1

For the Riemann’s θ\theta-function defined by (2.9), θ⁡(𝛈;𝟎|𝛕)\theta(\bm{\eta};\bm{0}|\bm{\tau}) is a NN-periodic wave solution of the single bilinear equation (2.11) if

∑m1∑m2⋯∑mN=−∞∞\displaystyle\qquad\sum_{m_{1}}\sum_{m_{2}}\cdots\sum_{m_{N}=-\infty}^{\infty}
F⁡[2​i​∑j=1N(mj−μj/2)​ωj,2​i​∑j=1N(mj−μj/2)​kj,⋯,λ]\displaystyle F[2i\sum_{j=1}^{N}(m_{j}-\mu_{j}/2)\omega_{j},2i\sum_{j=1}^{N}(m_{j}-\mu_{j}/2)k_{j},\cdots,\lambda]
×exp[−∑j,k=1N(mj−μj/2)τj,k(mk−μk/2)]=0,\displaystyle\qquad\times\exp[-\sum_{j,k=1}^{N}(m_{j}-\mu_{j}/2)\tau_{j,k}(m_{k}-\mu_{k}/2)]=0, (2.12)

for all possible combinations μ1=0,1\mu_{1}=0,1, μ2=0,1\mu_{2}=0,1, ⋯\cdots, μN=0,1\mu_{N}=0,1.

The proof of this lemma can be found in Refs. [18, 20, 29] .

Note that there are 2N2^{N} equations of type (2.12), and the total number of parameters ωj,kj​(j=1,2,⋯,N)\omega_{j},k_{j}(j=1,2,\cdots,N), λ\lambda, and τj,k​(1≤j,k≤N)\tau_{j,k}(1\leq j,k\leq N) is 2​N+1+N⁡(N+1)/22N+1+N(N+1)/2. Generally, the diagonal elements τj​j\tau_{jj} which influence the amplitudes, and the wave numbers kjk_{j}(or frequencies ωj\omega_{j}) are taken to be given parameters. Thus we have 2N2^{N} equations with 1+N⁡(N+1)/21+N(N+1)/2 unknowns. In the case of N=1,2N=1,2, we have the equal number of equations and unknown parameters while in the case of N≥3N\geq 3, the number of equations is larger than the number of unknown parameters, which means that this is an over-determined system.

2.2 Coupled KdV-type bilinear equations

We apply Lemma 2.1 to coupled KdV-type bilinear Eqs. (1.1)-(1.2). Note that, there is an auxiliary variable zz in this system. Therefore, the ηj\eta_{j} in the Riemann’s θ\theta-function (2.9) is defined by

ηj=ωjt+ljz+kjx+⋯+ηj0,j=1,2,⋯N.\eta_{j}=\omega_{j}t+l_{j}z+k_{j}x+\cdots+\eta_{j}^{0},\quad j=1,2,\cdots N. (2.13)

We have the following theorem.

Theorem 2.2

For the Riemann’s θ\theta-function defined by (2.9)-(2.13), θ⁡(𝛈;𝟎|𝛕)\theta(\bm{\eta};\bm{0}|\bm{\tau}) is a NN-periodic wave solution of the coupled bilinear equation (1.1)-(1.2) if

∑m1∑m2⋯∑mN=−∞∞F1[2i∑j=1N(mj−μj/2)ωj,\displaystyle\sum_{m_{1}}\sum_{m_{2}}\cdots\sum_{m_{N}=-\infty}^{\infty}F_{1}[2i\sum_{j=1}^{N}(m_{j}-\mu_{j}/2)\omega_{j},
2i∑j=1N(mj−μj/2)lj,2i∑j=1N(mj−μj/2)kj,⋯,c1]\displaystyle 2i\sum_{j=1}^{N}(m_{j}-\mu_{j}/2)l_{j},2i\sum_{j=1}^{N}(m_{j}-\mu_{j}/2)k_{j},\cdots,c_{1}]
×exp[−∑j,k=1N(mj−μj/2)τj,k(mk−μk/2)]=0,\displaystyle\quad\times\exp[-\sum_{j,k=1}^{N}(m_{j}-\mu_{j}/2)\tau_{j,k}(m_{k}-\mu_{k}/2)]=0, (2.14)
∑m1∑m2⋯∑mN=−∞∞F2[2i∑j=1N(mj−μj/2)ωj,\displaystyle\sum_{m_{1}}\sum_{m_{2}}\cdots\sum_{m_{N}=-\infty}^{\infty}F_{2}[2i\sum_{j=1}^{N}(m_{j}-\mu_{j}/2)\omega_{j},
2i∑j=1N(mj−μj/2)lj,2i∑j=1N(mj−μj/2)kj,⋯,c2]\displaystyle 2i\sum_{j=1}^{N}(m_{j}-\mu_{j}/2)l_{j},2i\sum_{j=1}^{N}(m_{j}-\mu_{j}/2)k_{j},\cdots,c_{2}]
×exp[−∑j,k=1N(mj−μj/2)τj,k(mk−μk/2)]=0,\displaystyle\quad\times\exp[-\sum_{j,k=1}^{N}(m_{j}-\mu_{j}/2)\tau_{j,k}(m_{k}-\mu_{k}/2)]=0, (2.15)

for all possible combinations μ1=0,1\mu_{1}=0,1, μ2=0,1\mu_{2}=0,1, ⋯\cdots, μN=0,1\mu_{N}=0,1.

The proof of this theorem is similar to that of Lemma 2.1 which is to substitute θ⁡(𝜼;𝟎|𝝉)\theta(\bm{\eta};\bm{0}|\bm{\tau}) into the coupled bilinear system (1.1)-(1.2) and simplify the formula with some bilinear identities and tedious calculations. We omit the details here.

Note that there are 2N+12^{N+1} equations, and the total number of parameters ωj,lj,kj​(j=1,2,⋯,N)\omega_{j},l_{j},k_{j}(j=1,2,\cdots,N), c1,c2c_{1},c_{2}, and τj,k​(1≤j,k≤N)\tau_{j,k}(1\leq j,k\leq N) is 3​N+2+N⁡(N+1)/23N+2+N(N+1)/2. With kjk_{j} and τj​j\tau_{jj} given, we obtain a nonlinear algebraic system of 2N+12^{N+1} equations with N+2+N⁡(N+1)/2N+2+N(N+1)/2 unknowns. Thus, for 11-periodic waves, we need to solve 44 parameters from 44 equations while for 22- and 33-periodic waves, we have to solve 77 and 1111 parameters from 88 and 1616 equations respectively.

3 Numerical scheme

In this section, we will introduce our numerical procedure to solve the unknown parameters from the nonlinear algebraic system(2.14)-(2.15). The main idea is to formulate the problem as a nonlinear least square problem and then use the Gauss-Newton method[43] to solve it.

For simplicity, we rewrite Eqs. (2.14)-(2.15) as

𝑯⁡(𝒙)=(H1,H2,⋯,H2N+1)T=0,{\bm{H(\bm{x}\bm{)}}}=(H_{1},H_{2},\cdots,H_{2^{N+1}})^{T}=0, (3.16)

where Hi=0​(i=1,2,⋯,2N+1)H_{i}=0(i=1,2,\cdots,2^{N+1}) is one of the equations in system (2.14)-(2.15) and 𝒙{\bm{x}} is a vector whose elements are the unknown parameters ωj\omega_{j}, ljl_{j}, τi​j​(i<j)\tau_{ij}(i<j) and c1,c2c_{1},c_{2}. The objective function of the nonlinear least square problem is

S⁡(𝒙)=12​∑n=12N+1Hn2​(𝒙)=12​𝑯​(𝒙)T​𝑯​(𝒙),S({\bm{x}})=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{n=1}^{2^{N+1}}H_{n}^{2}({\bm{x}})=\frac{1}{2}\bm{H}(\bm{x})^{T}\bm{H}(\bm{x}), (3.17)

Starting with an initial guess 𝒙[0]\bm{x}^{[0]}, the Gauss-Newton method proceeds by the iterations

𝒙[j+1]=𝒙[j]−(𝑱𝖳​𝑱)−1​𝑱𝖳​𝑯∣𝒙=𝒙[j],\bm{x}^{[j+1]}=\bm{x}^{[j]}-(\bm{J}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{J})^{-1}\bm{J}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{H}\mid_{\bm{x}=\bm{x}^{[j]}}, (3.18)

where 𝒙[j]\bm{x}^{[j]} (j≥1j\geq 1) is the jj-th iterative output and 𝑱\bm{J} is the Jacobian matrix of 𝑯\bm{H}, i.e.

𝑱=[∂Hi∂xj]i=1,…,2N+1;j=1,…,N+2+N⁡(N+1)/2\bm{J}=\left[\frac{\partial H_{i}}{\partial x_{j}}\right]_{i=1,\ldots,2^{N+1};j=1,\ldots,N+2+N(N+1)/2} (3.19)

This iterate process makes the objective function S⁡(𝒙)S({\bm{x}}) decay to zero. In the numerical experiments, if 𝑱𝖳​𝑱\bm{J}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{J} is near singular, change it to 𝑱𝖳​𝑱+10−6​𝑬\bm{J}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{J}+10^{-6}\bm{E} to modify the singularity, where 𝑬\bm{E} is the unit matrix.

The key of the procedure is the choice of initial guess 𝒙[0]\bm{x}^{[0]}. We suggest the following guidance to determine the initial guess. For given kjk_{j}, solve the initial guess ωj[0]\omega_{j}^{[0]} and lj[0]l_{j}^{[0]} from the equations

F1​(i​ωj[0],i​lj[0],i​kj,⋯,c1[0])=0,\displaystyle F_{1}(i\omega_{j}^{[0]},il_{j}^{[0]},ik_{j},\cdots,c_{1}^{[0]})=0, (3.20)
F2​(i​ωj[0],i​lj[0],i​kj,⋯,c2[0])=0,\displaystyle F_{2}(i\omega_{j}^{[0]},il_{j}^{[0]},ik_{j},\cdots,c_{2}^{[0]})=0, (3.21)

where the initial guess of c1[0]c_{1}^{[0]},c2[0]c_{2}^{[0]} are generally taken to be ±1\pm 1. In fact, if the initial guess 𝒙[0]\bm{x}^{[0]} satisfies Eqs. (3.20)-(3.21), the objective function S⁡(𝒙)S({\bm{x}}) will have a smaller initial value.

4 Numerical results

In this section, we use the numerical scheme to calculate 11-, 22- and 33-periodic wave solutions of the coupled Ramani Eqs. (1.4)-(1.5). This system was first proposed in Ref. [31], and its NN-solitons was known to be expressed by Pfaffians[38]. Some other properties and generalizations can be found in Refs. [39, 40, 41, 42]. As far as we know, there is no results about the periodic waves of this equation. It is worth mentioning that when v=0v=0, the coupled Ramani equation reduces to the following Ramani equation[30].

ux​x​x​x​x​x+15​ux​x​ux​x​x+15​ux​ux​x​x​x+45​ux2​ux​x\displaystyle u_{xxxxxx}+15u_{xx}u_{xxx}+15u_{x}u_{xxxx}+45u_{x}^{2}u_{xx}
−5​(ux​x​x​t+3​ux​x​ut+3​ux​ux​t)−5​ut​t=0.\displaystyle\quad-5(u_{xxxt}+3u_{xx}u_{t}+3u_{x}u_{xt})-5u_{tt}=0. (4.22)

Note that there are two constants u0u_{0} and v0v_{0} in the variable transformation (1.8) and u0u_{0} makes no difference to the bilinear equations while v0v_{0} does. Thus the numerical experiments will be carried out with v0=0v_{0}=0 and v0=1v_{0}=1 respectively. When plotting the profile of uu and vv, we will take u0=0u_{0}=0, ηj0=0\eta_{j}^{0}=0 and z=0z=0 without loss of generality.

All computations are carried out in Matlab R2013b on a computer with a 2.83 GHz CPU and 8 GB main memory. The termination condition for stopping the numerical iterative is ‖𝒙[j+1]−𝒙[j]‖2<10−14||{\bm{x}^{[j+1]}}-{\bm{x}^{[j]}}||_{2}<10^{-14} and ‖𝑯‖2<10−14||{\bm{H}}||_{2}<10^{-14} where ||⋅||2||\large{\cdot}||_{2} means 22-norm.

4.1 11-periodic waves

In the case of N=1N=1, according to Theorem 2.1, the problem is for given k1k_{1} and τ11\tau_{11}, to solve ω1\omega_{1}, l1l_{1}, c1c_{1} and c2c_{2} from a nonlinear algebraic system of 4 equations. Note that the coupled Ramani equation (1.4)-(1.5) are linear in c1c_{1} and c2c_{2}, and include terms Dt2D_{t}^{2} and Dz​DtD_{z}D_{t}. Thus after a tedious calculation, the nonlinear algebraic system reduces to a cubic equation of ω1\omega_{1}. Therefore, although very tediously but possibly, we are able to write out the exact solutions.

Here, instead of giving the exact expressions, we will present some 11-periodic wave solutions numerically by using the numerical scheme given in Sect. 3. When N=1N=1, the Jacobian matrix 𝑱\bm{J} is 4×44\times 4 and the Gauss-Newton iteration (3.18) reduces to the Newton iteration

𝒙[j+1]=𝒙[j]−𝑱−1​𝑯∣𝒙=𝒙[j].\bm{x}^{[j+1]}=\bm{x}^{[j]}-\bm{J}^{-1}\bm{H}\mid_{\bm{x}=\bm{x}^{[j]}}. (4.23)

The numerical experiments are successful and the errors of ‖𝑯‖2=0||{\bm{H}}||_{2}=0 hold within ∼10−15\sim 10^{-15}. See Tables 1-2 for several detailed examples. Fig. 1 shows the profiles of uu and vv of the first example in Table 1. This 11-periodic wave solution is periodic both in time and space. Actually, its spatial and temporal periods are 2​πk1=10\frac{2\pi}{k_{1}}=10 and 2​πl1=44.1235\frac{2\pi}{l_{1}}=44.1235 respectively. As shown in the Fig. 1, the profiles at t=0t=0 and t=44.1t=44.1 almost coincide for both uu and vv.

In the case of v0=0v_{0}=0, the numerical experiments may give some solutions of l1=0l_{1}=0(see the second example in Table 1) which means that the Riemann’s θ\theta-function is independent on zz. With the variable transformation (1.8), we have v=0v=0. Therefore, in this case, the solution uu reduces to the solution of the Ramani equation (4.22). The same goes in the numerical experiments of 22-periodic and 33-periodic waves which will be given below.

4.2 22-periodic waves

In this case, the nonlinear algebraic system (2.14)-(2.15) is an over-determined system of 8 equations with 7 unknowns. In our numerical experiments, the errors of ‖𝑯‖2=0||{\bm{H}}||_{2}=0 also hold within ∼10−15\sim 10^{-15}. See the detailed examples in Tables 3-4 and Figs. 2-3. These waves are periodic in space but only quasi-periodic in time. We also give an example of lj=0​(j=1,2)l_{j}=0(j=1,2)(see the last example in Table 3).

4.3 33-periodic waves

In the case of 33-periodic waves, the problem is a nonlinear system of 16 equations with 11 unknowns. Some detailed numerical examples are given in Tables 5-6. As shown in Figs. 4-5, the 33-periodic wave represents three waves interact with each other repeatedly.

In some cases, the numerical experiments will produce results with lj=0l_{j}=0(see the third example in Table 5). As we stated before, this kind of solutions will reduce to the solutions of the Ramani equation (4.22). However, as the iterative output 𝒙[j]{\bm{x}}^{[j]} tends to the exact solution, the corresponding matrix 𝑱𝖳​𝑱\bm{J}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{J} will be near-singular which will result in accuracy degradation. Actually, in the third example of Table 5, the error of ‖𝑯‖2=0||{\bm{H}}||_{2}=0 only holds within ∼10−9\sim 10^{-9} while in the other examples, the errors hold within ∼10−14\sim 10^{-14}.

5 Conclusion and discussion

A numerical process of calculating NN-periodic waves is presented and some numerical experiments are carried out with the coupled Ramani equation. The numerical results show that the process is efficient in calculating 11-, 22- and 33-periodic waves. Here we give two remarks.

Firstly, the numerical results are not unique since this is a nonlinear and over-determined system. For instance, in the third and forth examples in Table 5, with the same given parameters but the different initial guess, we obtain two different 33-periodic waves.

Secondly, there are many other soliton equations that can be transformed into the coupled bilinear KdV-type systems. For instance, the Hirota-Satsuma coupled KdV equation[32]

ut=14​ux​x​x+3​u​ux+3​(−ϕ2+ω)x,\displaystyle u_{t}=\frac{1}{4}u_{xxx}+3uu_{x}+3(-\phi^{2}+\omega)_{x}, (5.24)
ϕt=−12​ϕx​x​x−3​u​ϕx,\displaystyle\phi_{t}=-\frac{1}{2}\phi_{xxx}-3u\phi_{x}, (5.25)
ωt=12​ωx​x​x−3​u​ωx.\displaystyle\omega_{t}=\frac{1}{2}\omega_{xxx}-3u\omega_{x}. (5.26)

can be transformed into the bilinear form

(Dx​Dt−14​Dx4−34​Dz2)​f⋅f=0,\displaystyle(D_{x}D_{t}-\frac{1}{4}D_{x}^{4}-\frac{3}{4}D_{z}^{2})f\cdot f=0, (5.27)
Dz​(Dt+12​Dx3)​f⋅f=0,\displaystyle D_{z}(D_{t}+\frac{1}{2}D_{x}^{3})f\cdot f=0, (5.28)

by the dependent variable transformation

u=(ln​f)x​x,ϕ=12​fzf,ω=12​fz​zfu=(\mathrm{ln}f)_{xx},\quad\phi=\frac{1}{2}\frac{f_{z}}{f},\quad\omega=\frac{1}{2}\frac{f_{zz}}{f} (5.29)

where zz is an auxiliary variable, and the Camassa-Holm equation[33, 34]

ut+2​κ2​ux+3​u​ux−ux​x​t=2​ux​ux​x+u​ux​x​x,u_{t}+2\kappa^{2}u_{x}+3uu_{x}-u_{xxt}=2u_{x}u_{x}x+uu_{xxx}, (5.30)

can be transformed into

[Dy(Dt+2κ3Dy−κ2Dy2Dt)\displaystyle[D_{y}(D_{t}+2\kappa^{3}D_{y}-\kappa^{2}D_{y}^{2}D_{t})
+13κ2Dt(Dτ+Dy3)]f⋅f=0,\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad+\frac{1}{3}\kappa^{2}D_{t}(D_{\tau}+D_{y}^{3})]f\cdot f=0, (5.31)
Dy​(Dτ+Dy3)​f⋅f=0.\displaystyle D_{y}(D_{\tau}+D_{y}^{3})f\cdot f=0. (5.32)

with a so-called reciprocal transformation. Here τ\tau is an auxiliary variable and coordinate (y,t)(y,t) is generated from the reciprocal transformation. See details in Ref. [34].

Some discrete systems can also be transformed into this kind of bilinear equations. For example, the semi-discrete KdV equation given by Hirota and Ohta [35],

41+a2​un​dd​t​un=Δ3​M​un+6​un​Δ​M​un\displaystyle\frac{4}{1+a^{2}u_{n}}\frac{d}{dt}u_{n}=\Delta^{3}Mu_{n}+6u_{n}\Delta Mu_{n}
+a2​[Δ​M​(un​Δ2​un)+3​(Δ​M​un)​(Δ2​un)],\displaystyle\qquad\qquad+a^{2}[\Delta M(u_{n}\Delta^{2}u_{n})+3(\Delta Mu_{n})(\Delta^{2}u_{n})], (5.33)

can be transformed into

[2​a​Dz​sinh⁡(Dn2)−cosh⁡(3​Dn2)+cosh⁡(Dn2)]​f⋅f=0,\displaystyle[2aD_{z}\sinh(\frac{D_{n}}{2})-\cosh(\frac{3D_{n}}{2})+\cosh(\frac{D_{n}}{2})]f\cdot f=0,
(5.34)
(4​a2​Dt+3​Dz)​sinh⁡(Dn2)​f⋅f=Dz​sinh⁡(3​Dn2)​f⋅f,\displaystyle(4a^{2}D_{t}+3D_{z})\sinh(\frac{D_{n}}{2})f\cdot f=D_{z}\sinh(\frac{3D_{n}}{2})f\cdot f, (5.35)

with transformation

un=1a2​(fn+2​fn−1fn+1​fn−1).u_{n}=\frac{1}{a^{2}}(\frac{f_{n+2}f_{n-1}}{f_{n+1}f_{n}}-1). (5.36)

Our numerical process may also be applied to these soliton equations to study their NN-periodic wave solutions if some additional terms with arbitrary integral constants are introduced in these bilinear forms.
